session.title: Designing Our Stories: Technology, Culture & the Power of the Latino Narrative
session.description:
Technology doesn't just build products. It shapes how people experience, understand, and share the world.

For Latino communities in Detroit and throughout Michigan, storytelling is an essential part of preserving culture, building identity, creating connection, and making our contributions visible. From the stories we tell about our families and neighborhoods to the digital platforms, brands, products, and technologies we create, design and storytelling are deeply connected.

This session explores how Latino communities can use storytelling and technology to move from being represented by others to designing and sharing our own narratives.

The conversation will explore:

⚬	How culture influences the way we design technology and experiences
⚬	Why storytelling is a form of technology and community infrastructure
⚬	How Latino stories are represented, preserved, and sometimes overlooked
⚬	The role of UX, design, AI, media, and digital platforms in shaping cultural narratives
⚬	How entrepreneurs, technologists, designers, and community leaders can tell stories with greater intention
⚬	How Detroit's Latino communities can use technology to document and amplify stories across generations
⚬	What happens when we design technology with culture in mind, rather than designing culture out of technology

The big question: what changes when we stop asking technology to tell our stories, and start designing the technology, experiences, and platforms that let us tell them ourselves?

name: Umelo Onyejiaka
bio: Umelo Onyejiaka is a cloud and DevOps engineer, community builder, and the founder of DevOps Detroit. He holds multiple industry certifications including AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Professional, AWS Certified DevOps Engineer – Professional, Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA), and Terraform Associate. Beyond certifications, Umelo's work focuses on how people actually grow skills in the real world. He believes meaningful skill development happens faster and more sustainably in community through shared learning, mentorship, and exposure rather than in isolation. Through DevOps Detroit, he creates spaces where individuals can build practical technical skills, gain confidence, and see what's possible by learning alongside others on similar journeys. His approach centers on the idea that when people grow together, the entire ecosystem benefits.

session.title: AI Won't Replace Community: Why We Still Need to Learn Together
session.description:
AI is changing how we learn. Today, anyone can use AI to explain a technical concept, troubleshoot a problem, build a learning plan, or develop a new skill faster than ever before. But easier access to information doesn’t eliminate our need for each other.

This session explores why community remains essential in an AI-driven world. AI can provide answers, but community provides mentorship, accountability, shared experiences, collaboration, and access to opportunities that technology alone cannot replicate. We’ll explore how AI can strengthen—not replace—community-based learning and why the future of education and professional development should combine powerful AI tools with meaningful human connection.

Attendees will leave with a new perspective on AI: not as a replacement for learning together, but as a tool that can help communities learn, build, and grow together.

name: Greg Miller
bio: Greg Miller is the owner of Shrinkray Interactive, LLC, a web development studio focused on fixing broken sites, building accessible experiences, and designing custom interfaces that make complex data and workflows easy to use. He's built and maintained event sites for organizations like Compass Detroit, including Michigan DevFest and the Black History Month Summit, and speaks regularly at local networking events on making technical work approachable for non-technical audiences.

session.title: The 80/20 of Accessibility: Small Fixes, Big Impact
session.description:
"The 80/20 of Accessibility: Small Fixes, Big Impact" walks through the small number of fixes that solve most accessibility problems on the web — no WCAG memorization required. Using real screen reader demos, with audience participation, this talk breaks down high-impact issues and gives attendees practical, five-minute habits they can start using immediately, whether they're building their first project or their fiftieth. You don't need to be an expert to catch 80% of the problems — you need a checklist. 

What are we waiting for, let's get started today!

name: William Bowen
bio: I currently wear multiple professional hats as an IT specialist and a fitness instructor / enthusiast. On the IT side I have the responsibility for managing service orders, telecommunication contracts and services, along with support for iOS devices. I also have experience teaching networks, network security and software development. This work branches off to work I do with the National Society of Black Engineers (NSBE) and the Cyber Patriot program, which includes talks and tutorials on technology and computers. As a fitness enthusiast I have taught multiple boot camp classes that incorporate both strength and cardio training at different locations. This has led me to compete in multiple powerlifting meets with UPA and USAPL as well as physique with NPC. At this time I am also looking at different applications that incorporate fitness.

session.title: Getting Started with Project NOMAD
session.description: In an increasingly connected world, dependence on cloud infrastructure poses significant challenges during network blackouts, off-grid expeditions, remote work operations, and in environments with limited broadband access. Project NOMAD is a free, open-source, offline-first knowledge and education server designed to provide total digital autonomy and strict privacy.  This session introduces Project NOMAD, exploring how it turns standard hardware into a self-contained, air-gapped knowledge vault. Attendees will learn about its core architecture, practical use cases—ranging from emergency preparedness, remote medical references, and offline mapping to STEM education—and how to deploy local, private Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) AI without sending data to the cloud.

name: Andre Arbelaez
bio: Andre also is National Leader in the Hispanic community as the President & CEO of the Hispanic C-Suite Corporate Council (HC3), a non-profit organization, to increase the number of successful Hispanic executives for companies and executives in the Entertainment, Sports, and Technology sectors.  He is a member of the Board of Directors of the Michigan Council of Women in Technology (MCWT), the Michigan Science Center, while serving as Chairperson of the Advisory Board for Oakland University’s Decision and Information Sciences Department.  Andre was the former President of the Hispanic Information Technology Council (HITEC).

session.title: Detroit Latin Heritage Month Innovation Summit Panel Discussion
session.description:
Connect with leaders across Detroit’s design, engineering, and tech ecosystems for a panel focused on innovation, talent pathways, and cross-sector growth. Panelists unite to discuss career mobility, community architecture, and creative collaboration across industry boundaries.

Featured Perspectives
⚬	SHPE Detroit: Outlines the STEM talent pipeline, bridging students and professionals with corporate pathways in engineering.
⚬	Techqueria Detroit: Centers Latino/a/e technologists, advancing career mobility, workplace belonging, and professional community.
⚬	Latino Voices in Tech: Champions ecosystem visibility, representation, and advocacy through the power of storytelling.
⚬	Detroit Month of Design: Explores the intersection of design, placemaking, creativity, and cross-sector innovation.
⚬	Compass: Details innovation architecture, linking enterprise networks, startup founders, and local community initiatives.

name: Ricardo Tapia Vargas
bio: Ricardo is a Controls Engineer at Ford Motor Company and a recent Electrical Engineering graduate from the University of Detroit Mercy’s College of Engineering & Science. At Detroit Mercy, he served as President and Vice President of the SHPE UDM Student Chapter, led an 11-student senior design team competing in the Intelligent Ground Vehicle Competition, and was inducted into IEEE-Eta Kappa Nu (IEEE-HKN), the honor society of IEEE. A first-generation college graduate, Ricardo now serves as Co-Director of Future Engineers for SHPE Detroit, continuing his commitment to supporting the next generation of engineers.

session.title: Engineering Loteria
session.description:
Celebrate Hispanic Heritage Month through an interactive, culturally rooted spin on the classic game of chance. Replace the traditional chalupa and catrín with engineering icons, software terms, hardware components, and technical milestones. Attendees network, test their STEM trivia, and compete for prizes in a lively community atmosphere.
⚬	Interactive Gameplay: Custom Lotería cards spotlight engineering concepts, technical tools, and historic Hispanic innovators.
⚬	Community Connection: Connect students, seasoned technologists, and industry leaders across disciplines.
⚬	Prizes and Trivia: Earn recognition and take home gear while celebrating culture, craft, and technical problem-solving.

name: Raquel Estrada
bio:
Fixing what’s broken. Building what’s missing. Developing the people who make it last.

I’m a transformation and operational excellence leader with 12+ years of experience helping organizations turn strategy into practical, lasting improvements. Most of my work sits at the intersection of process, people, and execution—figuring out how things really work today, designing a better way forward, and helping teams make those changes stick.

Throughout my career I’ve worked across financial services, consumer goods, automotive, and manufacturing environments where processes are complex and teams have to work across functions to get results. I enjoy stepping into situations where processes are fragmented or unclear and helping bring structure, alignment, and momentum.

Some of the work I’ve led includes building an enterprise process transformation function at a bank, implementing BPM platforms to standardize processes and governance, running global continuous improvement initiatives, and developing internal capabilities so teams can sustain improvements on their own.
